after reviewing these datasets, we note that some of them
are of receipt type [12], [13], others consider a variety of
forms [14], [15], which differ slightly from a regular machi ne
written invoice. In [16], the authors propose a large datase t of
10000 synthetic invoices, speciﬁcally tailored for docume nt
analysis and understanding. However, these documents do no t
always reﬂect real-world scenarios where invoices are ofte n
photographed with mobile phones, introducing signiﬁcant d is-
tortions. We also notice that many of the datasets lack the
presence of stamp and signature components.
In order to ﬁll this gap and to effectively apply DL tech-
niques, we propose a novel, fully annotated dataset compose d
of real machine written invoice documents with various im-
perfections, such as blurriness, class imbalance, low-qua lity
phone-shot images, and varying formats. In our case study, w e
consider a machine written invoice document to be valid only
if it contains a stamp, a signature, and certain selected ﬁel ds.
After collecting and annotating the dataset, we select the m ost
relevant DL-based approaches for implementation and bench -
marking. We progressively evaluate and improve the results
until obtaining a robust pipeline that maximizes accuracy a nd
reliability, while maintaining reasonable performance.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In
Section II, we present the material considered and the metho ds
proposed. The results are reported and discussed in Section III,
while Section IV concludes the paper and discusses the futur e
perspectives.
II. M ATERIALS AND METHODS
In this section, we present the materials, detailing the dat a
collection and processing pipeline, and then describe the m eth-
ods, including the selection of the most recent and relevant
models for implementation. Since invoice validation consi sts
of two main tasks, we divide our work into two independent
steps: keyword detection and object detection. The adopted
training pipeline is shown in Figure 1, which shows that
keyword detection is preceded by an OCR phase, which allows
for an OCR-augmented dataset. For object detection, we aim
to verify the presence of signatures and stamps to ensure the
authenticity of ﬁnancial documents.
Fig. 1: Adopted training pipeline.
A. Materials
We outline the dataset used for our DL pipeline by ﬁrst
describing the data annotation process, followed by data
augmentation and preparation.
1) Data annotation:
We collected 381 real ﬁnancial documents, of which 84%
(320 documents) are invoices. Among these, 240 are machine-
written. We manually annotated the documents with bounding
boxes around the necessary elements to establish the validi ty
of the invoices, as shown in Table I. All classes are represen ted
as bounding boxes, except for a boolean attribute indicatin g
whether handwriting is present.
TABLE I: Annotated dataset description.
Class Description
Title Document type (e.g., invoice, receipt, etc.).
Client Client name.
Stamp Stamp for document authenticity.
Signature Signature for document authenticity.
Date Issue date, different formats.
Total Total label.
Total V alue Total numeric value.
Handwritten True if handwritten (not machine-written).
An example of an annotated document is shown in Figure
2. For conﬁdentiality reasons, some parts of the ﬁnancial
documents have been blurred.
Fig. 2: Example of an annotated document.
Our dataset includes various real invoices; many are dis-
torted due to mobile phone capture as depicted in Figure 3, an d
some are handwritten, potentially appearing skewed during
capture, as illustrated by Figure 4.
This work focuses on the processing of digital invoices,
since handwritten invoices are sparse in the current datase t, and
present additional challenges for augmentation and proces sing.
